entries.c14644265d53612b36d8d601efd7eece39f0e17f: <div sID="gen13186" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="142" osisID="Ps.142" sID="Ps.142"/> <div eID="gen13186" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13187" type="x-p"/> This psalm is a prayer, the substance of which David offered up to God when he was forced by Saul to take shelter in a cave, and which he afterwards penned in this form. Here is, I. The complaint he makes to God (<reference osisRef="Ps.142.1-Ps.142.2">ver. 1, 2</reference>) of the subtlety, strength, and malice, of his enemies (<reference osisRef="Ps.142.3">ver. 3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.142.6">6</reference>), and the coldness and indifference of his friends, <reference osisRef="Ps.142.4">ver. 4</reference>. II. The comfort he takes in God that he knew his case (<reference osisRef="Ps.142.3">ver. 3</reference>) and was his refuge, <reference osisRef="Ps.142.5">ver. 5</reference>. III. His expectation from God that he would hear and deliver him, <reference osisRef="Ps.142.6-Ps.142.7">ver. 6, 7</reference>. IV His expectation from the righteous that they would join with him in praises, <reference osisRef="Ps.142.7">ver. 7</reference>. Those that are troubled in mind, body, or estate, may, in singing this psalm (if they sing it in some measure with David's spirit), both warrant his complaints and fetch in his comforts.
entries.d817424716d22600c549c7db60c4eaddf6554607: <div eID="gen13187" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">David's Complaints.</title> <div sID="gen13188" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> I cried unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> with my voice; with my voice unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> did I make my supplication. <hi type="super">2</hi> I poured out my complaint before him; I showed before him my trouble. <hi type="super">3</hi> When my spirit was overwhelmed within me, then thou knewest my path. In the way wherein I walked have they privily laid a snare for me. <div eID="gen13188" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13189" type="x-p"/> Whether it was in the cave of <hi type="italic">Adullam,</hi> or that of <hi type="italic">Engedi,</hi> that David prayed this prayer, is not material; it is plain that he was in distress. It was a great disgrace to so great a soldier, so great a courtier, to be put to such shifts for his own safety, and a great terror to be so hotly pursued and every moment in expectation of death; yet then he had such a presence of mind as to pray this prayer, and, wherever he was, still had his religion about him. Prayers and tears were his weapons, and, when he durst not stretch forth his hands against his prince, he lifted them up to his God. There is no cave so deep, so dark, but we may out of it send up our prayers, and our souls in prayer, to God. He calls this prayer <hi type="italic">Maschil—a psalm of instruction,</hi> because of the good lessons he had himself learnt in the cave, learnt on his knees, which he desired to teach others. In these verses observe, <div eID="gen13189" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13190" type="x-p"/> I. How David complained to God, <reference osisRef="Ps.142.1-Ps.142.2">v. 1, 2</reference>. When the danger was over he was not ashamed to own (as great spirits sometimes are) the fright he had been in and the application he had made to God. Let no men of the first rank think it any diminution or disparagement to them, when they are in affliction, to cry to God, and to cry like children to their parents when any thing frightens them. <hi type="italic">David poured out his complaint,</hi> which denotes a free and full complaint; he was copious and particular in it. His heart was as full of his grievances as it could hold, but he made himself easy by pouring them out before the Lord; and this he did with great fervency: <hi type="italic">He cried unto the Lord with his voice,</hi> with the voice of his mind (so some think), for, being hidden in the cave, he durst not speak with an audible voice, lest that should betray him; but mental prayer is vocal to God, and he hears the groanings which cannot, or dare not, be uttered, <reference osisRef="Rom.8.26">Rom. viii. 26</reference>. Two things David laid open to God, in this complaint:—1. His distress. He exhibited a remonstrance or memorial of his case: <hi type="italic">I showed before him my trouble,</hi> and all the circumstances of it. He did not prescribe to God, nor show him his trouble, as if God did not know it without his showing; but as one that put a confidence in God, desired to keep up communion with him, and was willing to refer himself entirely to him, he unbosomed himself to him, humbly laid the matter before him, and then cheerfully left it with him. We are apt to show our trouble too much to ourselves, aggravating it, and poring upon it, which does us no service, whereas by showing it to God we might cast the care upon him who careth for us, and thereby ease ourselves. Nor should we allow of any complaint to ourselves or others which we cannot with due decency and sincerity of devotion make to God, and stand to before him. 2. His desire. When he made his complaint he <hi type="italic">made his supplication</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.142.1">v. 1</reference>), not claiming relief as a debt, but humbly begging it as a favour. Complainants must be suppliants, for God will be sought unto. <div eID="gen13190" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13191" type="x-p"/> II. What he complained of: "<hi type="italic">In the way wherein I walked,</hi> suspecting no danger, <hi type="italic">have they privily laid a snare for me,</hi> to entrap me." Saul gave Michal his daughter to David on purpose that she might be <hi type="italic">a snare to him,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.21">1 Sam. xviii. 21</reference>. This he complains of to God, that every thing was done with a design against him. If he had gone out of his way, and met with snares, he might have thanked himself; but when he met with them in the way of his duty he might with humble boldness tell God of them. <div eID="gen13191" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13192" type="x-p"/> III. What comforted him in the midst of these complaints (<reference osisRef="Ps.142.3">v. 3</reference>): "<hi type="italic">When my spirit was overwhelmed within me,</hi> and ready to sink under the burden of grief and fear, when I was quite at a loss and ready to despair, <hi type="italic">then thou knewest my path,</hi> that is, then it was a pleasure to me to think that thou knewest it. Thou knewest my sincerity, the right path which I have walked in, and that I am not such a one as my persecutors represent me. Thou knewest my condition in all the particulars of it; when my spirit was so overwhelmed that I could not distinctly show it, this comforted me, that thou knewest it, <reference osisRef="Job.23.10">Job xxiii. 10</reference>. Thou knewest it, that is, thou didst protect, preserve, and secure it," <reference osisRef="Ps.31.7">Ps. xxxi. 7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.2.7">Deut. ii. 7</reference>.
entries.3b1303f3f3613dd086b0a0e67ba0bbfde984a9d7: <div eID="gen13192" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Complaints and Petitions.</title> <div sID="gen13193" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">4</hi> I looked on <hi type="italic">my</hi> right hand, and beheld, but <hi type="italic">there was</hi> no man that would know me: refuge failed me; no man cared for my soul. <hi type="super">5</hi> I cried unto thee, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> : I said, Thou <hi type="italic">art</hi> my refuge <hi type="italic">and</hi> my portion in the land of the living. <hi type="super">6</hi> Attend unto my cry; for I am brought very low: deliver me from my persecutors; for they are stronger than I. <hi type="super">7</hi> Bring my soul out of prison, that I may praise thy name: the righteous shall compass me about; for thou shalt deal bountifully with me. <div eID="gen13193" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13194" type="x-p"/> The psalmist here tells us, for our instruction, 1. How he was disowned and deserted by his friends, <reference osisRef="Ps.142.4">v. 4</reference>. When he was in favour at court he seemed to have a great interest, but when he was made an out-law, and it was dangerous for any one to harbour him (witness Ahimelech's fate), then <hi type="italic">no man would know him,</hi> but every body was shy of him. He looked <hi type="italic">on his right hand</hi> for an advocate (<reference osisRef="Ps.109.31">Ps. cix. 31</reference>), some friend or other to speak a good word for him; but, since Jonathan's appearing for him had like to have cost him his life, nobody was willing to venture in defence of his innocency, but all were ready to say they knew nothing of the matter. He looked round to see if any would open their doors to him; but <hi type="italic">refuge failed him.</hi> None of all his old friends would give him a night's lodging, or direct him to any place of secresy and safety. How many good men have been deceived by such swallow-friends, who are gone when winter comes! David's life was exceedingly precious, and yet, when he was unjustly proscribed, <hi type="italic">no man cared for it,</hi> nor would move a hand for the protection of it. Herein he was a type of Christ, who, in his sufferings for us, was forsaken of all men, even of his own disciples, and trod the wine-press alone, for there was <hi type="italic">none to help, none to uphold,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.63.5">Isa. lxiii. 5</reference>. 2. How he then found satisfaction in God, <reference osisRef="Ps.142.5">v. 5</reference>. Lovers and friends stood aloof from him, and it was in vain to call to them. "But," said he, "<hi type="italic">I cried unto thee, O Lord!</hi> who knowest me, and carest for me, when none else will, and wilt not fail me nor forsake me when men do;" for God is constant in his love. David tells us what he said to God in the cave: "<hi type="italic">Thou art my refuge and my portion in the land of the living;</hi> I depend upon thee to be so, <hi type="italic">my refuge</hi> to save me from being miserable, <hi type="italic">my portion</hi> to make me happy. The cave I am in is but a poor refuge. Lord, <hi type="italic">thy name</hi> is the <hi type="italic">strong tower</hi> that <hi type="italic">I run into.</hi> Thou art <hi type="italic">my refuge,</hi> in whom alone I shall think myself safe. The crown I am in hopes of is but a poor portion; I can never think myself well provided for till I know that <hi type="italic">the Lord is the portion of my inheritance and of my cup.</hi>" Those who in sincerity take the Lord for their God shall find him all-sufficient both as a refuge and as a portion, so that, as no evil shall hurt them, so no good shall be wanting to them; and they may humbly claim their interest: "<hi type="italic">Lord, thou art my refuge and my portion;</hi> every thing else is a refuge of lies and a portion of no value. Thou art so <hi type="italic">in the land of the living,</hi> that is, while I live and have my being, whether in this world or in a better." There is enough in God to answer all the necessities of this present time. We live in a world of dangers and wants; but what danger need we fear if God is our refuge, or what wants if he be our portion? Heaven, which alone deserves to be called <hi type="italic">the land of the living,</hi> will be to all believers both a refuge and a portion. 3. How, in this satisfaction, he addressed himself to God (<reference osisRef="Ps.142.5-Ps.142.6">v. 5, 6</reference>): "Lord, give a gracious <hi type="italic">ear to my cry,</hi> the cry of my affliction, the cry of my supplication, for <hi type="italic">I am brought very low,</hi> and, if thou help me not, I shall be quite sunk. Lord, <hi type="italic">deliver me from my persecutors,</hi> either tie their hands or turn their hearts, break their power or blast their projects, restrain them or rescue me, <hi type="italic">for they are stronger than I,</hi> and it will be thy honour to take part with the weakest. Deliver me from them, or I shall be ruined by them, for I am not yet myself a match for them. Lord, <hi type="italic">bring my soul out of prison,</hi> not only bring me safe out of this cave, but bring me out of all my perplexities." We may apply it spiritually: the souls of good men are often straitened by doubts and fears, cramped and fettered through the weakness of faith and the prevalency of corruption; and it is then their duty and interest to apply themselves to God, and beg of him to set them at liberty and to enlarge their hearts, that they may <hi type="italic">run the way of his commandments.</hi> 4. How much he expected his deliverance would redound to the glory of God. (1.) By his own thanksgivings, into which his present complaints would then be turned: "<hi type="italic">Bring my soul out of prison,</hi> not that I may enjoy myself and my friends and live at ease, no, nor that I may secure my country, but <hi type="italic">that I may praise thy name.</hi>" This we should have an eye to, in all our prayers to God for deliverance out of trouble, that we may have occasion to praise God and may live to his praise. This is the greatest comfort of temporal mercies that they furnish us with matter, and give us opportunity, for the excellent duty of praise. (2.) By the thanksgivings of many on his behalf (<reference osisRef="2Cor.1.11">2 Cor. i. 11</reference>): "When I am enlarged <hi type="italic">the righteous shall encompass me about;</hi> for <hi type="italic">my cause they shall make thee a crown of praise,</hi> so the Chaldee. They shall flock about me to congratulate me on my deliverance, to hear my experiences, and to receive (Maschil) instructions from me; they shall encompass me, to join with me in my thanksgivings, <hi type="italic">because thou shalt</hi> have dealt <hi type="italic">bountifully with me.</hi>" Note, The mercies of others ought to be the matter of our praises to God; and the praises of others, on our behalf, ought to be both desired and rejoiced in by us.  <chapter eID="Ps.142"/> <div eID="gen13194" type="x-p"/>

entries.1d6b751219cae48b62a6d36ff99829ab171f2be3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7096"/><title type="x-s2">PSALM 142</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ps.142.1-Ps.142.7">Psa 142:1-7</reference>. Maschil--(See on <reference osisRef="Ps.32.1">Psa 32:1</reference>, title). When he was in the cave--either of Adullam (<reference osisRef="1Sam.22.1">1Sa 22:1</reference>), or En-gedi (<reference osisRef="1Sam.24.3">1Sa 24:3</reference>). This does not mean that the Psalm was composed in the cave, but that the precarious mode of life, of which his refuge in caves was a striking illustration, occasioned the complaint, which constitutes the first part of the Psalm and furnishes the reason for the prayer with which it concludes, and which, as the prominent characteristic, gives its name.</title> <div sID="gen10880" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7096"/><hi type="bold">1. with my voice--</hi>audibly, because earnestly. <div eID="gen10880" type="x-p"/>
entries.2d9f6713cf2b48ff74298902e822fc9b9d5f620f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7097"/><div sID="gen10881" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7097"/>2. (Compare <reference osisRef="Ps.62.8">Psa 62:8</reference>).<div eID="gen10881" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10882" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I poured out my complaint--</hi>or, "a sad musing." <div eID="gen10882" type="x-p"/>
entries.e2e8f63f04467788eadb750190aed43f9e1661a2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7098"/><div sID="gen10883" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7098"/><hi type="bold">3. thou knewest ... path--</hi>The appeal is indicative of conscious innocence; knowest it to be right, and that my affliction is owing to the snares of enemies, and is not deserved (compare <reference osisRef="Ps.42.4">Psa 42:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.61.2">61:2</reference>). <div eID="gen10883" type="x-p"/>
entries.4d74c70955df3af88396d477a977d7f1c37f464a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7099"/><div sID="gen10884" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7099"/>4. Utter desolation is meant.<div eID="gen10884" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10885" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">right hand--</hi>the place of a protector (<reference osisRef="Ps.110.5">Psa 110:5</reference>).<div eID="gen10885" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10886" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cared for--</hi>literally, "sought after," to do good. <div eID="gen10886" type="x-p"/>
entries.dec1d639b57f50c92f907fa723cd1b105659ffb9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7100"/><div sID="gen10887" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7100"/>5. (Compare <reference osisRef="Ps.31.14">Psa 31:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.62.7">62:7</reference>). <div eID="gen10887" type="x-p"/>

entries.6bd7f782b4bcc8aadab5390a750c19d682c5d50d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv7102"/><div sID="gen10889" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv7102"/>7. (Compare <reference osisRef="Ps.25.17">Psa 25:17</reference>).<div eID="gen10889" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10890" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">that I may praise--</hi>literally, "for praising," or, "that Thy name may be praised," that is, by the righteous, who shall surround me with sympathizing joy (<reference osisRef="Ps.35.27">Psa 35:27</reference>). <chapter eID="Ps.142"/>

entries.c6d0e32a0520fe76068ff8cc8ba53d801eb3ed24: <div eID="gen23401" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen23402" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen23403" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen23403" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen23402" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen23404" type="x-p"/> The psalmist, in great distress and difficulty, calls upon God, <reference osisRef="Psa.142.1-Psa.142.7">Psa 142:1-7</reference>. <div eID="gen23404" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23405" type="x-p"/> The title says, "An Instruction of David," or a Psalm of David giving instruction; "A Prayer when he was in the cave." <div eID="gen23405" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23406" type="x-p"/> David was twice in great peril in caves. <div eID="gen23406" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23407" type="x-p"/> 1. At the cave of Adullam, when he fled from Achish, king of Gath, 1 Samuel 22. <div eID="gen23407" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23408" type="x-p"/> 2. When he was in the cave of En-gedi, where he had taken refuge from the pursuit of Saul; and the latter, without knowing that David was in it, had gone into it on some necessary occasion, 1 Samuel 24. <div eID="gen23408" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23409" type="x-p"/> If the inscription can be depended on, the cave of En-gedi is the most likely of the two, for the scene laid here. But were there doubts concerning the legitimacy of the title, I should refer the Psalm to the state of the captives in Babylon, to which a great part of the Psalms refer. Bishop Horsley calls it "A Prayer of the Messiah taken and deserted." It may be so: but where is the evidence, except in the conjectural system of Origen. <div eID="gen23409" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23410" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen23410" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23411" type="x-p"/> I cried unto the Lord - See on <reference osisRef="Psa.141.1">Psa 141:1</reference> (note).
entries.fdeba7026a3d1a3b8d84d434da1c7ece62ef28ad: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen23411" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23412" type="x-p"/> Then thou knewest my path - When Saul and his army were about the cave in which I was hidden, thou knewest my path - that I had then no way of escape but by miracle: but thou didst not permit them to know that I was wholly in their power.
entries.807d3728c4536d42da7d5021b5faa072639b8dac: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen23412" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23413" type="x-p"/> There was no man, that would know me - This has been applied to the time in which our Lord was deserted by his disciples. As to the case of David in the cave of En-gedi, he had no refuge: for what were the handful of men that were with him to Saul and his army?
entries.548bc65019a089612ada6b5474b409c5cf66a350: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen23413" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23414" type="x-p"/> Thou art my refuge - Even in these most disastrous circumstances, I will put my trust in thee.
entries.d5fcfadb391b61262d245e55a3e78233886dfdc9: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen23414" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23415" type="x-p"/> I am brought very low - Never was I so near total ruin before. <div eID="gen23415" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23416" type="x-p"/> Deliver me from my persecutors - They are now in full possession of the only means of my escape. <div eID="gen23416" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23417" type="x-p"/> They are stronger than I - What am I and my men against this well-appointed armed multitude, with their king at their head.
entries.ece3cd79bc4b13df40e8895fc8b16ab183c4f33f: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen23417" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23418" type="x-p"/> Bring my soul out of prison - Bring נפשי naphshi, my life, out of this cave in which it is now imprisoned; Saul and his men being in possession of the entrance. <div eID="gen23418" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23419" type="x-p"/> The righteous shall compass me about - יכתרו yachtiru, they shall crown me; perhaps meaning that the pious Jews, on the death of Saul, would cheerfully join together to make him king, being convinced that God, by his bountiful dealings with him, intended that it should be so. The old Psalter, which is imperfect from the twenty-frst verse of Psalm 119 to the end of <reference osisRef="Psa.141.1-Psa.141.10">Psa 141:1-10</reference>, concludes this Psalm thus: "Lede my saule oute of corruption of my body; that corrupcion is bodely pyne, in whilk my saule is anguyst; after that in Godes house, Sal al be louyng (praising) of the."  <chapter eID="Ps.142"/> <div eID="gen23419" type="x-p"/>

entries.4c62b0ff55607f7e654439fc6780e03607b653bf: <div eID="gen10302" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">Cry Sent Forth from the Prison to the Best of Friends</title> <div sID="gen10303" type="x-p"/> This the last of the eight Davidic Psalms, which are derived by their inscriptions from the time of the persecution by Saul (vid., on Ps 34), is inscribed: <hi type="italic">A Meditation by David, when he was in the cave, a Prayer</hi>. Of these eight Psalms, <reference osisRef="Ps.52.1-Ps.52.9">Psa 52:1-9</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ps.54.1-Ps.54.7">Psa 54:1-7</reference> also bear the name of <hi type="italic">Maskı̂l</hi> (vid., on <reference osisRef="Ps.32.1-Ps.32.11">Psa 32:1-11</reference>); and in this instance תּפּלּה (which occurs besides as an inscription only in <reference osisRef="Ps.90.1">Psa 90:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.102.1">Psa 102:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.3.1">Psa 3:1</reference>) is further added, which looks like an explanation of the word <hi type="italic">maskı̂l</hi> (not in use out of the range of Psalm-poetry). The article of במערה, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.57.1">Psa 57:1</reference>, points to the cave of Adullam (1 Sam. 22) or the cave of Engedi (1 Sam. 24), which latter, starting from a narrow concealed entrance, forms such a labyrinthine maze of passages and vaults that the torches and lines of explorers have not to the present time been able to reach the extremities of it. <div eID="gen10303" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10304" type="x-p"/> The Psalm does not contain any sure signs of a post-Davidic age; still it appears throughout to be an imitation of older models, and pre-eminently by means of Psa 142:2. (cf. Psa 77:2.) and <reference osisRef="Ps.142.4">Psa 142:4</reference> (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.77.4">Psa 77:4</reference>) it comes into a relation of dependence to Ps 77, which is also noticeable in <reference osisRef="Ps.143.1-Ps.143.12">Psa 143:1-12</reference> (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.142.5">Psa 142:5</reference> with Psa 77:12.). The referring back of the two Psalms to David comes under one and the same judgment.
entries.d60de0590c9d33606520d7e11e14a55e1418e73d: <reference osisRef="Ps.142.1-Ps.142.3">Psa 142:1-3</reference> <div eID="gen10304" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10305" type="x-p"/> The emphasis of the first two lines rests upon אל־ה. Forsaken by all created beings, he confides in Jahve. He turns to Him in pathetic and importunate prayer (זעק, the parallel word being התחנּן, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.30.9">Psa 30:9</reference>), and that not merely inwardly (<reference osisRef="Exod.14.15">Exo 14:15</reference>), but with his voice (vid., on <reference osisRef="Ps.3.5">Psa 3:5</reference>) - for audible prayer reacts soothingly, strengtheningly, and sanctifyingly upon the praying one - he pours out before Him his trouble which distracts his thoughts (שׁפך שׂיח as in <reference osisRef="Ps.102.1">Psa 102:1</reference>, cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.62.9">Psa 62:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.64.2">Psa 64:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.1.16">1Sa 1:16</reference>), he lays open before Him everything that burdens and distresses him. Not as though He did not also know it without all this; on the contrary, when his spirit (רוּחי as in <reference osisRef="Ps.143.4">Psa 143:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.77.4">Psa 77:4</reference>, cf. נפשׁי <reference osisRef="Jonah.2.7">Jon 2:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.107.5">Psa 107:5</reference>, לבּי <reference osisRef="Ps.61.3">Psa 61:3</reference>) within him (עלי, see <reference osisRef="Ps.42.5">Psa 42:5</reference>) is enshrouded and languishes, just this is his consolation, that Jahve is intimately acquainted with his way together with the dangers that threaten him at every step, and therefore also understands how to estimate the title (right) and meaning of his complaints. The <hi type="italic">Waw</hi> of ואתּה is the same as in 1Ki 8:36, cf. Ps 35. Instead of saying: then I comfort myself with the fact that, etc., he at once declares the fact with which he comforts himself. Supposing this to be the case, there is no need for any alteration of the text in order to get over that which is apparently incongruous in the relation of <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.142.4">Psa 142:4</reference></hi> to <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.142.4">Psa 142:4</reference></hi>.
entries.24a734fb6a8c91097a2fcea5f559eb477176e31f: <reference osisRef="Ps.142.6-Ps.142.7">Psa 142:6-7</reference> <div eID="gen10306" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10307" type="x-p"/> His request now ascends all the more confident of being answered, and becomes calm, being well-grounded in his feebleness and the superiority of his enemies, and aiming at the glorifying of the divine Name. In <reference osisRef="Ps.142.7">Psa 142:7</reference> רנּתי calls to mind <reference osisRef="Ps.17.1">Psa 17:1</reference>; the first confirmation, <reference osisRef="Ps.79.8">Psa 79:8</reference>, and the second, Psa 18:18. But this is the only passage in the whole Psalter where the poet designates the “distress” in which he finds himself as a prison (מסגּר). V. 8 <hi type="italic">b</hi> brings the whole congregation of the righteous in in the praising of the divine Name. The poet therefore does not after all find himself so absolutely alone, as it might seem according to Psa 142:5. He is far from regarding himself as the only righteous person. He is only a member of a community or church whose destiny is interwoven with his own, and which will glory in his deliverance as its own; for “if one member is honoured, all the members rejoice with it” (<reference osisRef="1Cor.12.26">1Co 12:26</reference>). We understand the differently interpreted יכתּירוּ after this “rejoicing with” (συγχαίρει). The lxx, Syriac, and Aquilaz render: the righteous wait for me; but to wait is כּתּר and not הכתּיר. The modern versions, on the other hand, almost universally, like Luther after Felix Pratensis, render: the righteous shall surround me (flock about me), in connection with which, as Hengstenberg observes, בּי denotes the tender sympathy they fell with him: crowding closely upon me. But there is no instance of a verb of surrounding (אפף, סבב, סבב, עוּד, עטר, הקּיף) taking בּ; the accusative stands with הכתּיר in <reference osisRef="Hab.1.4">Hab 1:4</reference>, and כּתּר in <reference osisRef="Ps.22.13">Psa 22:13</reference>, in the signification <hi type="italic">cingere</hi>. Symmachus (although erroneously rendering: τὸ ὄνομά σου στεφανώσονται δίκαιοι), Jerome (<hi type="italic">in me coronabuntur justi</hi>), Parchon, Aben-Ezra, Coccejus, and others, rightly take יכתּירוּ as a denominative from כּתר, to put on a crown or to crown (cf. <reference osisRef="Prov.14.18">Pro 14:18</reference>): on account of me the righteous shall adorn themselves as with crowns, i.e., shall triumph, that Thou dealest bountifully with me (an echo of <reference osisRef="Ps.13.6">Psa 13:6</reference>). According to passages like Ps 64:11; <reference osisRef="Ps.40.17">Psa 40:17</reference>, one might have expected בּו instead of בּי. But the close of Ps 22 (Psa 22:23.), cf. Psa 140:12., shows that בי is also admissible. The very fact that David contemplates his own destiny and the destiny of his foes in a not merely ideal but foreordainedly causal connection with the general end of the two powers that stand opposed to one another in the world, belongs to the characteristic impress of the Psalms of David that come from the time of Saul’s persecution.  <chapter eID="Ps.142"/> <div eID="gen10307" type="x-p"/>

entries.38c2b28fb30214b5a9b87a04eee735f653aa38d3:
PSALM 142
When Saul came into the cave where David lay concealed, this saint of God might upon such an occurrence have been either thrown into consternation, or led by his alarm into some unwarrantable step, it being common for persons in despair either to be prostrated with dismay, or driven into frenzy. But it appears from this Psalm that David retained his composure, relying with assured confidence upon God, and resigning himself to vows and prayers instead of taking any unauthorized steps.
A Prayer of David, giving instruction when he was in the cave.
In the history of David we read particularly of the two caves in which he took shelter, that of Adullam, (1 Samuel 22:1,) and that of En-gedi, (1 Samuel 24:3.) The latter is generally supposed to be the cave here
Psalm 142:1-4
1. I cried to Jehovah with my voice, with my voice to Jehovah I made supplication. 2. I pour out my meditation before his face: I tell my affliction before his face. 3. When my spirit was perplexed within me, and thou knewest my path: in the way wherein I walked they laid a snare for me. 4. On looking to the right hand, and perceiving, none would know me, refuge failed me, there was none seeking after my soul.
 
1. I cried
In the Hebrew the verb is in the future — “I will cry;” but as that language has no present tense, it frequently uses for it the past and future promiscuously. Bishop Horne, therefore, renders in the present all the verbs in this Psalm, which Calvin translates in the past, except the verbs in the two first verses, which he renders in the future. Translators, however, in general concur with Calvin, and we think justly, the Psalm, as we conceive, being a recollection of the substance of the prayers he addressed to God while in the cave of En-gedi, but which it cannot be supposed he had then an opportunity of committing to writing.
to Jehovah, etc. It showed singular presence of mind in David that he was not paralyzed with fear, or that he did not in a paroxysm of fury take vengeance upon his enemy, as he easily might have done; and that he was not actuated by despair to take away his life, but composedly addressed himself to the exercise of prayer. There was good reason why the title should have been affixed to the Psalm to note this circumstance, and David had good grounds for mentioning how he commended himself to God. Surrounded by the army of Saul, and hemmed in by destruction on every side, how was it possible for him to have spared so implacable an enemy, had he not been fortified against the strongest temptations by prayer? The repetition he makes use of indicates his having prayed with earnestness, so as to be impervious to every assault of temptation.
He tells us still more clearly in the next verse that he disburdened his ears unto God. To pour out one’s thoughts and tell over his afflictions implies the reverse of those perplexing anxieties which men brood over inwardly to their own distress, and by which they torture themselves, and are chafed by their afflictions rather than led to God; or it implies the reverse of those frantic exclamations to which others give utterance who find no comfort in the superintending providence and care of God. In short, we are left to infer that while he did not give way before men to loud and senseless lamentations, neither did he suffer himself to be tormented with inward and suppressed cares, but made known his grief’s with unsuspecting confidence to the Lord.

Poole.heading:
PSAL. CXLII. 
                     Or, A Psalm of David giving instruction.
                      Maschil of David; a prayer when he was in the cave Either that of Adullam, 1 Sam. 22. or that of Engedi, 1 Sam. 24. There he meditated this Psalm, which afterwards he more accurately composed and committed to writing..
